description: Microbes, protists and fungi: bacteria, archaea, single-celled eukaryotes, red algae and the fungal kingdom, including the yeasts, moulds and mushrooms people have domesticated.

nodes.name: Proteobacteria
nodes.summary: A huge and varied phylum of bacteria with thin, double-layered cell walls. It includes gut microbes, plant partners and some of history's most feared germs.
facts: The name comes from Proteus, a Greek sea god who could change shape, because these bacteria come in so many forms.
Salmonella, Vibrio (cholera) and the plague bacterium all belong here.

nodes.name: E. coli
nodes.summary: A rod-shaped bacterium that lives in the guts of warm-blooded animals, including you. Most strains are harmless, and some help by making vitamin K2. It is also the best-studied living thing on Earth.
facts: In good conditions E. coli can divide every 20 minutes.
Since 1988 one lab has followed the same E. coli populations for more than 75,000 generations. Along the way, one population evolved the ability to eat citrate.
Genetically modified E. coli has made human insulin for people with diabetes since the early 1980s.

treatments.note: common first choice for bladder infections
one-dose option for bladder infections
if local strains are not resistant
for O157:H7 food poisoning, where antibiotics can raise the risk of kidney damage

us.note: Found everywhere: it lives in nearly everyone’s gut. Harmful strains spread through undercooked beef, raw produce and unwashed hands.

medicine.resistance: More and more E. coli carry ESBL genes that break down penicillins and most cephalosporins, so doctors often test which drugs still work before choosing one.

nodes.name: Plague bacterium
nodes.summary: The cause of plague, spread mainly by fleas that live on rats and other rodents. It evolved only a few thousand years ago from a much milder gut bacterium.
facts: The Black Death (1346–1353) killed perhaps a third to half of everyone in Europe.
Its DNA has been recovered from Stone Age and Bronze Age skeletons around 5,000 years old.
A few genetic changes let it survive inside fleas and block their guts, so starving fleas bite again and again.

treatments.note: first-line
first-line, and the original plague cure
first-line, can be taken by mouth
also used to prevent plague after exposure

us.note: About 7 human cases a year, mostly in northern New Mexico, northern Arizona and southern Colorado, then California, southern Oregon and far western Nevada. Prairie dogs, ground squirrels and their fleas carry it.

nodes.name: Salmonella
nodes.summary: A gut bacterium that causes food poisoning, often from undercooked chicken, eggs or contaminated produce. One type, Salmonella Typhi, causes typhoid fever.
facts: It is named after Daniel Salmon, a US veterinary scientist, although his assistant Theobald Smith did much of the work.
“Typhoid Mary” Mallon, a cook in New York in the early 1900s, carried typhoid without ever feeling sick and infected dozens of people.

treatments.note: most food poisoning clears up without antibiotics
for severe cases or typhoid
for severe cases or typhoid
for severe cases, if the strain is not resistant

us.note: Found everywhere, causing about 1.35 million US infections a year, with a peak in summer.

medicine.resistance: Drug-resistant strains are rising, including typhoid strains that resist nearly everything except a few drugs such as azithromycin and carbapenems.

nodes.name: Spotted fever bacterium
nodes.summary: A tiny bacterium that can only live inside cells and spreads through tick bites. It causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which can be deadly if not treated quickly.
facts: Despite the name, most cases today come from the Southeast and South-Central states, not the Rocky Mountains.
It was identified by Howard Ricketts in Montana in the early 1900s. He later died of typhus, a related disease he was studying.

treatments.note: first choice for all ages, including young children
rarely used backup

us.note: More than half of cases come from North Carolina, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Tennessee and Missouri. Brown dog ticks have also caused outbreaks on tribal lands in Arizona.

nodes.name: Firmicutes
nodes.summary: Mostly thick-walled bacteria, many of which can survive as tough spores. The phylum covers yogurt and cheese makers, important gut residents and dangerous toxin producers.
facts: Spores of one member of this group were revived from lake mud about 7,000 years old.
Bacillota and Bacteroidota are the two biggest groups of bacteria in the human gut.

nodes.name: Yogurt bacterium
nodes.summary: A lactic-acid bacterium that adapted to life in milk. It turns milk sugar into lactic acid, which thickens and sours milk into yogurt.
facts: Its genome is slowly shrinking. Living in milk, where food is easy, it has been losing genes it no longer needs.
It works in a team with Streptococcus thermophilus. Each partner makes nutrients that help the other grow faster.
nodes.origin: Shaped without anyone meaning to, as herders across the Balkans and Middle East kept fermenting milk over thousands of years. The Bulgarian doctor Stamen Grigorov identified it in 1905, and starter cultures are now grown industrially around the world.

nodes.name: Clostridium
nodes.summary: Spore-forming bacteria that cannot stand oxygen. Most of them quietly break down dead material in soil and guts, but a few make the deadliest toxins known.
facts: Botulinum toxin from C. botulinum is among the most poisonous substances known. Tiny doses of it are sold as Botox.
Tetanus is caused by C. tetani spores getting into deep wounds.
In World War I, Chaim Weizmann used C. acetobutylicum to make acetone for British explosives.

treatments.note: neutralises the toxin; the main treatment for botulism and tetanus
for tetanus
with surgery, for gas gangrene
added for gas gangrene to shut down toxin production

us.note: The spores are in soil everywhere. Vaccines have made tetanus rare (about 30 US cases a year). Most US botulism is in babies, which is why infants under one should not eat honey.

nodes.name: C. diff
nodes.summary: A spore-forming gut bacterium that strikes when antibiotics wipe out a person’s normal gut microbes. Its toxins cause severe diarrhoea and an inflamed colon, mostly in hospitals and nursing homes.
facts: It used to be called Clostridium difficile, but in 2016 it was moved to a genus of its own.
For infections that keep coming back, one of the best treatments is a transplant of healthy gut microbes from a donor’s stool.
Its spores survive alcohol hand gel, so hospitals rely on soap and water to wash it away.

treatments.note: first choice, by mouth
by mouth; the main alternative
for infections that keep coming back

us.note: Found in every state, causing roughly half a million infections a year, mostly linked to hospitals, nursing homes and recent antibiotic use.

medicine.resistance: C. diff naturally shrugs off many common antibiotics. Those drugs kill its gut competitors, which is how it gets its chance.

nodes.name: Staph
nodes.summary: A round bacterium carried harmlessly in the nose of about 1 in 3 people. When it gets into a cut or the blood it can cause boils, pneumonia and deadly bloodstream infections.
facts: Its name means “golden bunch of grapes”: the cells cluster like grapes and its colonies look golden.
Penicillin-resistant staph turned up within a few years of penicillin coming into use in the 1940s.
MRSA, the methicillin-resistant kind, was first reported in 1961, just two years after methicillin went on sale.

treatments.note: for staph that is not resistant (MSSA)
for serious MRSA infections, by IV
for MRSA skin infections
for MRSA bloodstream infections

us.note: Found everywhere: in hospitals, and in everyday places like gyms, locker rooms and schools.

medicine.resistance: MRSA resists methicillin and nearly all penicillin-like drugs, so doctors switch to others such as vancomycin. A few strains are now partly resistant to vancomycin too.

nodes.name: Strep A
nodes.summary: The bacterium behind strep throat, impetigo and scarlet fever. Rarely, it invades deep tissue and causes so-called flesh-eating disease.
facts: More than 80 years after penicillin arrived, Strep A still has not become resistant to it.
Treating strep throat with antibiotics helps prevent rheumatic fever, which can damage the heart.

treatments.note: first choice
first choice, and easier for kids to take
for a mild penicillin allergy
for a serious penicillin allergy

us.note: Found everywhere. Strep throat is most common in school-age children during the colder months.

medicine.resistance: Penicillin still works, but resistance to azithromycin and its relatives is growing, so they are kept as backups.

nodes.name: Actinobacteria
nodes.summary: Bacteria that often grow as branching threads, a bit like miniature fungi. They are master chemists of the soil and the source of most of our antibiotics.
facts: The bacteria that cause tuberculosis and leprosy belong to this phylum.
The bacteria on your skin that help cause acne are actinobacteria too.

nodes.name: Streptomyces
nodes.summary: Soil bacteria that grow like tiny moulds and make chemical weapons against their rivals. Doctors have turned those weapons into hundreds of medicines.
facts: About two thirds of natural antibiotics used in medicine come from actinobacteria, most of them from Streptomyces.
The earthy smell after rain is mostly geosmin, made by Streptomyces. Your nose can detect a few parts per trillion.
Streptomycin, isolated from a Streptomyces in 1943, was the first drug that could cure tuberculosis.

nodes.name: TB bacterium
nodes.summary: The bacterium that causes tuberculosis (TB). It spreads through the air, mainly attacks the lungs, and kills more people worldwide than almost any other single germ.
facts: It is a cousin of Streptomyces, the soil bacteria that gave us streptomycin, the first drug that could cure TB.
Its thick, waxy coat makes it slow-growing and hard for drugs to get into, so treatment takes months.
About a quarter of the world’s people carry TB in a sleeping (latent) form that is not contagious.

treatments.note: part of the 4-drug “RIPE” combo, taken for about 6 months
part of RIPE
part of RIPE, first 2 months
part of RIPE, first 2 months

us.note: Found in every state. California, Texas, New York and Florida report the most cases, and Alaska and Hawaii have the highest rates per person.

medicine.resistance: Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) shrugs off the two strongest drugs, isoniazid and rifampin, and needs newer treatments. Taking every dose matters, because skipped doses let resistant bacteria take over.

nodes.name: Spirochaetes
nodes.summary: Corkscrew-shaped bacteria that drill through thick liquids by twisting their whole body. Their tails (flagella) run inside the cell instead of sticking out.
facts: Lyme disease and syphilis are both caused by spirochaetes.
Spirochaetes living in termite guts help their hosts digest wood.

nodes.name: Lyme disease bacterium
nodes.summary: The corkscrew bacterium behind Lyme disease, the most common tick-borne disease in the US. Blacklegged (deer) ticks pick it up from mice and other small animals and pass it to people.
facts: It is named after Lyme, Connecticut, where a puzzling cluster of childhood arthritis cases was investigated in the 1970s.
Ötzi the Iceman, who died in the Alps about 5,300 years ago, carried its DNA, so the disease is far older than its name.
It barely needs iron, which almost every other living thing depends on. That lets it dodge one of the body’s tricks for starving germs.

treatments.note: first choice
during pregnancy, or if doxycycline is not an option
another option

us.note: Most cases come from the Northeast, the mid-Atlantic and the upper Midwest, where blacklegged ticks live, with a few on the Pacific coast. Its range keeps spreading.

nodes.name: Syphilis bacterium
nodes.summary: A thin corkscrew bacterium that causes syphilis, which spreads through sex and from a pregnant mother to her baby. Untreated, it can hide in the body for years and damage the heart, brain and eyes.
facts: For more than a century scientists could not grow it in a lab dish. They finally managed it in 2018, using a layer of rabbit cells.
Where syphilis came from has been argued about for 500 years. Ancient DNA studies published in 2024 suggest its family of bacteria first spread in the Americas.

diseases: Congenital syphilis (passed to a baby before birth)

treatments.note: first choice; one shot treats early syphilis
for penicillin allergy, but not during pregnancy

us.note: Found in every state. Cases have climbed sharply since the early 2000s, and babies born with syphilis rose more than tenfold between 2012 and 2022.

medicine.resistance: More than 80 years on, penicillin still works every time. But it has become resistant to azithromycin, so that drug is no longer recommended.

nodes.name: Chlamydiae
nodes.summary: Bacteria that can only survive inside other cells, where they steal energy and nutrients from their host. Some infect humans, and others live inside amoebas.
facts: Chlamydiae have probably been living inside eukaryotic cells for at least 700 million years.
The eye infection trachoma, caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, is the world's leading infectious cause of blindness.

nodes.name: Chlamydia
nodes.summary: A tiny bacterium that lives inside human cells. It causes the most commonly reported bacterial sexually transmitted infection in the US, and in poorer countries it causes the blinding eye disease trachoma.
facts: Most people who have it feel no symptoms, which is why doctors screen for it.
It switches between two forms: a tough, spore-like body that travels between cells, and a bigger form that multiplies inside them.

treatments.note: first choice, a 7-day course
a single dose; used in pregnancy and against trachoma

us.note: Found in every state, with about 1.6 million US cases reported in 2022, more than half of them among people aged 15 to 24.

nodes.name: Prochlorococcus
nodes.summary: The smallest known photosynthetic cell and the most abundant one on Earth. It floats in sunlit oceans in numbers too huge to picture.
facts: There are roughly 3 octillion (3 followed by 27 zeros) Prochlorococcus cells in the oceans.
Even though it is so common, nobody found it until 1988.

nodes.name: Crenarchaea
nodes.summary: Archaea famous for living in boiling, acidic hot springs. Some of their relatives turned out to be among the most common cells in the open ocean.
facts: Sulfolobus lives in Yellowstone's sulfur springs at around 80 °C, in water as acidic as lemon juice.
Ammonia-eating members of this group make up as much as a fifth of the tiny cells in the sea.

nodes.name: Euryarchaeota
nodes.summary: A sprawling group of archaea that includes methane-makers, salt-lovers and microbes that thrive in boiling water at deep-sea vents.
facts: Pyrococcus furiosus, the rushing fireball, grows best at 100 °C.

nodes.name: Methanogens
nodes.summary: Archaea that live without oxygen and release methane gas as their waste. They live in swamps, rice paddies, deep rocks and animal guts, including yours.
facts: Methanopyrus kandleri strain 116 can still multiply at 122 °C, a record for life.
Methanobrevibacter smithii is the most common archaeon in the human gut.
Making methane is one of the oldest ways of life. It may go back more than 3.5 billion years.

nodes.name: Salt-loving archaea
nodes.summary: Archaea that need water several times saltier than the sea. Their reddish pigments paint salt ponds and some lakes pink and red.
facts: Many of them use bacteriorhodopsin, a purple protein that pumps charged particles when hit by light. It is a simple kind of solar power that works without chlorophyll.
They pack their cells with potassium so water is not sucked out of them by the brine.

nodes.name: Square archaeon
nodes.summary: A microbe shaped like a tiny, ultra-thin square postage stamp. It floats in salt-saturated brine pools using gas bubbles inside its cell.
facts: Its cells are about 2 micrometres across but only about 0.1 micrometres thick.
It was discovered in 1980 in a brine pool on the Sinai Peninsula by the microbiologist Anthony Walsby.

nodes.name: Lokiarchaeota
nodes.summary: The first Asgard archaea ever found, known at first only from DNA in deep-sea mud. They carry many genes for building internal skeletons and membranes that were once thought to exist only in complex cells.
facts: They were named in 2015 after Loki's Castle, a hydrothermal vent field between Greenland and Norway.
It took Japanese scientists about 12 years to grow one of them, Prometheoarchaeum, in the lab. It grows long, tentacle-like arms.

nodes.name: Discoba
nodes.summary: An ancient branch of single-celled eukaryotes that includes sunlight-eating Euglena, sleeping-sickness parasites and amoebas that can grow tails.
facts: Many members have a groove on their underside that sweeps in food, one reason they were once lumped together as excavates.

nodes.name: Euglena
nodes.summary: A green, swimming single cell that photosynthesises like a plant in the light and can soak up food from the water in the dark. Its chloroplasts came from a green alga that an ancestor swallowed.
facts: A red eyespot helps it steer toward light.
Its chloroplasts are wrapped in three membranes, a leftover sign of the swallowed alga.

nodes.name: Trypanosomes
nodes.summary: Wriggling blood parasites that cause sleeping sickness (spread by tsetse flies) and Chagas disease (spread by kissing bugs).
facts: T. brucei keeps one step ahead of your immune system by swapping its protein coat, drawing on a library of more than a thousand coat genes.
Its single mitochondrion holds a tangled chain-mail of thousands of interlocked DNA rings.

nodes.name: Metamonads
nodes.summary: Single-celled eukaryotes that live where there is little or no oxygen, often in guts. Their mitochondria have shrunk to tiny stubs, and some have lost them completely.
facts: In 2016 Monocercomonoides became the first eukaryote known to have no mitochondria at all.
Metamonads living in termite guts help the termites digest wood.

nodes.name: Giardia
nodes.summary: A gut parasite that seems to stare back through the microscope: its two nuclei look like eyes. It clamps onto your intestine with a sucker-like disc and causes beaver fever.
facts: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first saw Giardia in 1681, in a sample of his own diarrhoea.
It has two nuclei, and each one holds a full set of genes.

nodes.name: Amoebozoa
nodes.summary: Blob-like amoebas that crawl by pushing out lobes of their own body, plus the extraordinary slime moulds.
facts: The dysentery parasite Entamoeba histolytica is an amoebozoan.

nodes.name: Social amoeba
nodes.summary: Lives as separate amoebas until food runs out. Then up to 100,000 of them gather into a slug that crawls toward light and builds a tiny stalk topped with spores.
facts: About a fifth of the cells die to form the stalk, sacrificing themselves so the others can spread as spores.
Some strains carry bacteria along with them and seed them in their new home, like tiny farmers.

nodes.name: Many-headed slime mould
nodes.summary: A bright yellow, brainless blob that is one giant cell with millions of nuclei. It can find the shortest path through a maze to reach food.
facts: When oat flakes were placed like the cities around Tokyo, it grew a network strikingly similar to the real rail system.
It has hundreds of different mating types, not just two sexes.

nodes.name: Choanoflagellates
nodes.summary: The closest living relatives of animals: single cells with one tail and a collar of tiny fingers that catch bacteria. They look almost exactly like the feeding cells of sponges.
facts: Salpingoeca rosetta forms rosette-shaped colonies when it detects a molecule made by certain bacteria, a hint of how animals' many-celled bodies may have begun.
They carry genes for cell-sticking proteins that were once thought to exist only in animals.

nodes.name: Stramenopiles
nodes.summary: A huge branch ranging from microscopic diatoms to 45-metre kelp, plus fungus-like water moulds. Their swimming cells have a tail covered in stiff hairs.
facts: The name means straw hairs, after the hollow hairs on their front flagellum.

nodes.name: Golden-brown algae
nodes.summary: The photosynthetic stramenopiles: diatoms, kelps and many golden algae. Their ancestor took over the chloroplast of a swallowed red alga, a stolen solar panel inside a stolen solar panel.
facts: Their chloroplasts are wrapped in four membranes, which records that two rounds of swallowing happened.
A golden pigment called fucoxanthin gives them their brown and olive colours.

nodes.name: Diatoms
nodes.summary: Single-celled algae that live inside intricate glass boxes made of silica. Together they produce about a fifth of the oxygen made on Earth.
facts: Alfred Nobel used diatomaceous earth, made of fossil diatom shells, to make dynamite safe to handle.
Dust from a dried-up diatom lakebed in the Sahara blows across the Atlantic and fertilises the Amazon rainforest.

nodes.name: Brown algae
nodes.summary: Seaweeds such as kelps, wracks and sargassum. They evolved large, many-celled bodies on their own, completely separately from plants and animals.
facts: Alginate from brown algae thickens ice cream, toothpaste and salad dressing.
The Sargasso Sea is named after floating mats of Sargassum and is the only sea with no coastline.

nodes.name: Giant kelp
nodes.summary: The largest alga in the world. It grows up from the sea floor in underwater forests that shelter fish, seals and sea otters.
facts: It can grow about 50 centimetres in a single day and reach over 45 metres long.
Each blade has a gas-filled bulb that floats it up toward the sunlight.
Sea otters protect kelp forests by eating the sea urchins that would otherwise mow them down.

nodes.name: Water moulds
nodes.summary: They grow in threads just like fungi, but they are actually cousins of diatoms and kelp. Many are devastating plant diseases.
facts: Their cell walls are made of cellulose like plants, not chitin like real fungi.
Phytophthora ramorum causes sudden oak death, which has killed millions of trees in California and Oregon.

nodes.name: Potato blight
nodes.summary: The water mould that rots potato and tomato plants. It caused the Irish Potato Famine of 1845–1852, when about a million people died and another million emigrated.
facts: Phytophthora is Greek for plant destroyer.
Its spores can swim through films of water on leaves using two tails.
DNA from 19th-century herbarium leaves revealed the exact strain that caused the famine.

nodes.name: Alveolates
nodes.summary: Protists with a layer of tiny flattened sacs just under their surface. They include the glowing dinoflagellates, the malaria parasite and the ciliates.

nodes.name: Dinoflagellates
nodes.summary: Spinning plankton with two tails, one wrapped around their middle. Some make breaking waves glow electric blue at night, some cause toxic red tides, and some live inside corals and feed them.
facts: Dino means whirling in Greek, from the way they spin as they swim.
When coral reefs bleach, it is because stressed corals expel their dinoflagellate partners.
Some dinoflagellates have genomes dozens of times larger than yours.

nodes.name: Apicomplexans
nodes.summary: Parasites with a special toolkit at their tip for breaking into cells. Their ancestors could photosynthesise, and they still carry a useless leftover chloroplast.
facts: Toxoplasma, another apicomplexan, makes infected rats lose their fear of cat smell, which helps it get back into cats.
Chromera, a photosynthetic close relative discovered in corals in 2008, shows what their ancestors were like.

nodes.name: Malaria parasite
nodes.summary: The deadliest malaria parasite, spread by Anopheles mosquitoes. It hides inside red blood cells and still kills more than half a million people a year, mostly young children in Africa.
facts: It jumped to humans from a gorilla parasite.
The sickle-cell gene became common in parts of Africa because carrying one copy protects against malaria.
Tu Youyou won a 2015 Nobel Prize for artemisinin, a malaria drug she found in a 1,600-year-old Chinese herbal text.

nodes.name: Ciliates
nodes.summary: Fast, hairy single cells covered in thousands of beating cilia. They have two kinds of nucleus: a small one for passing on genes and a big one for running the cell.
facts: Work on the ciliate Tetrahymena led to two Nobel Prizes, for discovering RNA enzymes and how chromosome tips (telomeres) are protected.
Cut a Stentor into pieces and even small pieces can regrow into whole cells, as long as each holds a bit of the nucleus.

nodes.name: Paramecium
nodes.summary: A slipper-shaped pond dweller that sweeps bacteria into its mouth groove and swims by rowing thousands of cilia. It is a favourite of school microscopes.
facts: It can fire tiny harpoons called trichocysts to fend off predators.
Star-shaped pumps called contractile vacuoles bail out extra water so it does not burst.

nodes.name: Rhizaria
nodes.summary: Amoeba-like protists that reach out with long, thread-like arms, often from inside elaborate shells of chalk or glass.
facts: Gromia sphaerica, a grape-sized single cell on the deep sea floor, seems to roll slowly across the mud, leaving tracks.

nodes.name: Foraminifera
nodes.summary: Single cells that build chambered shells of chalk or glued sand. Their fossil shells pile up in their trillions to make limestone and record ancient ocean temperatures.
facts: The limestone of the Egyptian pyramids is packed with coin-shaped fossil forams called Nummulites. The geographer Strabo thought they were the workers' leftover lentils.
Deep-sea xenophyophores are forams that can grow 20 centimetres across, yet each one is a single cell.

nodes.name: Radiolarians
nodes.summary: Ocean plankton with breathtaking glass skeletons shaped like snowflakes, lanterns and spiky stars.
facts: Ernst Haeckel's drawings of radiolarians in Art Forms in Nature (1904) inspired Art Nouveau designers.
Their fossil skeletons have been found in rocks over 500 million years old.

nodes.name: Red algae
nodes.summary: Seaweeds coloured red by a pigment that soaks up blue light, which lets them grow deeper than any other seaweed. Their chloroplasts were later stolen by diatoms, kelp and many other algae.
facts: A red alga has been found growing 268 metres below the sea surface, where almost no light reaches.
Agar for lab dishes and carrageenan for ice cream both come from red algae.
Chalky coralline red algae help cement coral reefs together.

nodes.name: Bangiomorpha
nodes.summary: A tiny red seaweed fossilised in Arctic Canadian rocks about 1.05 billion years old. It is the oldest known organism that clearly reproduced sexually.
facts: Its name is a joke: pubescens refers to it being the first creature known to have reached sexual maturity.
It is one of the oldest fossils that can be placed in a group still alive today.

nodes.name: Nori
nodes.summary: The red seaweed pressed into the dark green sheets wrapped around sushi. It is one of the world's most valuable farmed seaweeds.
facts: British scientist Kathleen Drew-Baker worked out nori's hidden life stage, which lives inside seashells, and saved Japan's nori farms. She is honoured there every April as the Mother of the Sea.
Some Japanese people carry gut bacteria with a seaweed-digesting gene that their ancestors picked up from marine bacteria.
nodes.origin: Gathered in Japan for over a thousand years and farmed on nets in Tokyo Bay since the Edo period (1600s). Nori sheets were first made the way washi paper is made. Seeding nets with spores from shells after 1949 turned it into a huge industry.

nodes.name: Chytrids
nodes.summary: Some of the most ancient-looking fungi. Their spores swim with a single tail, a reminder that fungi and animals share a swimming ancestor.
facts: Many chytrids live in water and decompose pollen, plant debris and the shells of insects.

nodes.name: Frog-killing chytrid
nodes.summary: A chytrid that infects the skin of frogs and salamanders, which they breathe through. It has caused the greatest loss of biodiversity known to be caused by a single disease.
facts: It has helped drive declines in over 500 amphibian species, and about 90 species are thought to have gone extinct.
Its deadliest strain probably spread out of East Asia during the 20th century through the global trade in amphibians.

nodes.name: Pin moulds
nodes.summary: Fast-growing moulds that cover old bread and fruit in fuzz topped with tiny black spore balls. A Rhizopus mould turns soybeans into tempeh.
facts: Pilobolus, a dung fungus, fires its spore packet up to 2.5 metres. At launch it speeds up about 20,000 times faster than gravity.
The rice-seedling-killing toxin of one Rhizopus is actually made by bacteria living inside the fungus.

nodes.name: Mucor
nodes.summary: The classic pin mould: a white fuzz that sprouts on forgotten food, with each thread topped by a round black ball of spores.
facts: Some Mucor species can switch between growing as threads and growing as budding yeast-like cells.

nodes.name: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi
nodes.summary: Fungi that grow inside plant roots and trade water and minerals for sugar. They partner with most land plants and may have helped plants move onto land in the first place.
facts: About 70% of land plant species form this partnership.
The same partnership is preserved in 407-million-year-old fossil plants from the Rhynie chert in Scotland.
They cannot live without a plant partner, so they cannot be grown on their own in a dish.

nodes.name: Sac fungi
nodes.summary: The largest group of fungi. Their spores form inside microscopic sacs, and the group includes yeasts, moulds, morels, truffles and most of the fungi in lichens.
facts: About two thirds of all named fungus species are sac fungi.
Each sac usually holds exactly eight spores.

nodes.name: Baker's & brewer's yeast
nodes.summary: A single-celled fungus that eats sugar and releases carbon dioxide and alcohol. The gas makes bread rise and the alcohol makes beer and wine.
facts: In 1996 it became the first eukaryote to have its whole genome read.
When scientists swapped hundreds of essential yeast genes for their human versions, nearly half still kept the yeast alive, after a billion years apart.
nodes.origin: Wild ancestors live on trees in East Asian forests. People were unknowingly using it for fermented drinks in China 9,000 years ago, and for bread and beer in Egypt and Mesopotamia soon after. Separate domesticated lines arose for wine, beer, bread and sake, and Louis Pasteur showed in the 1850s–60s that it is alive.

nodes.name: Patagonian yeast
nodes.summary: A cold-loving wild yeast discovered in 2011 growing on beech-tree galls in Patagonia, South America. It turned out to be the missing other parent of lager yeast.
facts: It has since been found in Tibet, China and North America too.

nodes.name: Lager yeast
nodes.summary: A hybrid of brewer's yeast and the cold-tolerant Patagonian yeast. It can ferment in chilly Bavarian cellars, which gives lager its crisp taste.
facts: In 1883 Emil Christian Hansen at the Carlsberg brewery grew the first pure culture of lager yeast.
Lager is the most consumed style of beer in the world.
nodes.origin: Born about 500 years ago, probably in Bavaria, when a cerevisiae ale yeast crossed with a stray eubayanus. Brewers fermenting beer in cold caves over winter kept selecting it without knowing it.

nodes.name: Penicillium
nodes.summary: The blue-green mould on old oranges. One species gave us penicillin, the first mass-produced antibiotic, and others make blue cheese and Camembert.
facts: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed a mould killing bacteria on a dish he had left out over his holiday.
Penicillin for World War II came from a strain found on a mouldy cantaloupe in Peoria, Illinois.
The blue veins in Roquefort and Stilton are Penicillium roqueforti, a mould domesticated in cheese caves.

nodes.name: Koji mould
nodes.summary: A domesticated mould that breaks down starch and protein into sugars and savoury flavours. It is the secret ingredient behind soy sauce, miso and sake.
facts: In 2006 the Brewing Society of Japan named it Japan's national fungus.
Its wild ancestor, Aspergillus flavus, makes a powerful poison. Domestication broke the genes that make the poison.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in China from wild Aspergillus flavus over several thousand years, as people kept mould-covered grain (koji) to start fermentations. It reached Japan more than a thousand years ago, and koji makers there have sold it as a starter for centuries.

nodes.name: Morels
nodes.summary: Prized wild mushrooms with a hollow, honeycomb-pitted cap. Foragers guard their secret morel spots closely.
facts: Some morels sprout in huge numbers the spring after a forest fire.
Raw morels are toxic, so they must always be cooked.
The morel is Minnesota's official state mushroom.

nodes.name: Black truffle
nodes.summary: An underground fungus that grows on oak and hazel roots. Since it cannot release spores into the air, it gives off a powerful smell so that animals dig it up and spread its spores.
facts: Truffles contain androstenol, a scent also found in boar saliva, which may be why female pigs are so good at finding them.
Many truffle hunters now use dogs, because pigs tend to eat the truffles.

nodes.name: Zombie-ant fungus
nodes.summary: A fungus that infects carpenter ants and takes control of their bodies. It makes them climb a plant and clamp their jaws onto a leaf vein, then grows a stalk out of their head to rain spores on ants below.
facts: Fossil leaves 48 million years old from Germany show the same death-grip bite marks.
The fungus wraps around the ant's muscles but leaves its brain largely intact.
It inspired the zombie fungus in the video game The Last of Us.

nodes.name: Club fungi
nodes.summary: Mushrooms, puffballs, bracket fungi and rusts. They grow their spores on tiny club-shaped cells, often on the gills under a mushroom cap.
facts: White-rot club fungi are the champions at breaking down lignin, the tough material in wood.
A single mushroom can release billions of spores in a day.

nodes.name: Common mushroom
nodes.summary: The supermarket mushroom. Button mushrooms, cremini and portobellos are all the same species, picked at different ages or from different strains.
facts: The wild form has a brown cap and still grows in grasslands across the Northern Hemisphere.
nodes.origin: First cultivated around Paris in the mid-1600s, later in the old limestone quarries under the city, which is why the French still call it champignon de Paris.

nodes.name: White button mushroom
nodes.summary: The pure white mushroom in most supermarkets. Its white colour traces back to a mutant clump that turned up on a single farm a century ago.
facts: Kennett Square, Pennsylvania, calls itself the mushroom capital of the world.
nodes.origin: In 1926 a Pennsylvania mushroom farmer found a clump of white mushrooms in a bed of brown ones and cloned it. Shoppers preferred the clean white look, and Dutch breeders later crossed it with off-white strains to make the high-yield hybrids grown today.

nodes.name: Fly agaric
nodes.summary: The red-capped, white-spotted toadstool from fairy tales and video games. It is poisonous, and it lives in partnership with the roots of birch, pine and spruce trees.
facts: Its name comes from an old trick: pieces soaked in milk were used to attract and kill flies.
The white spots are bits of a veil that covered the young mushroom, and rain can wash them off.

nodes.name: Honey fungus
nodes.summary: A tree-killing fungus that spreads underground with black, bootlace-like cords. One individual in Oregon is among the largest and oldest living things on Earth.
facts: The Oregon giant is thought to be between 2,400 and 8,650 years old.
Honey fungi are one cause of foxfire, the eerie glow given off by some rotting wood at night.

nodes.name: Shiitake
nodes.summary: A savoury mushroom that grows on dead hardwood logs. It is the most-produced edible mushroom in the world.
facts: Its name means mushroom of the shii tree, a Japanese relative of the oak.
Eating it raw or undercooked can cause a rare, whip-like skin rash.
nodes.origin: First cultivated in China around 1,000 years ago by cutting notches in fallen logs so spores could get in. Growing it in sawdust blocks has made it a global crop since the late 1900s.

nodes.name: Rust fungi
nodes.summary: Plant parasites that cover leaves in rusty orange spots. They are some of the most dangerous diseases of wheat, coffee and other crops.
facts: Some rusts make five different kinds of spores and need two different host plants to finish their life cycle.
Coffee rust wiped out Ceylon's coffee farms in the 1870s, so British planters switched to tea, and Sri Lanka has been famous for tea ever since.
Wheat stem rust also infects barberry bushes, so the USA tried to dig up every barberry in its wheat belt after 1918.

nodes.name: Prototaxites
nodes.summary: A mysterious giant that towered up to 8 metres over the first land plants, which were mostly shin-high. Its tree-like trunks were made of tangled tubes, not wood, and many scientists think it was an enormous fungus.
facts: Chemical signals in its fossils show it fed on other organisms rather than sunlight.
A 2025 study argued it was not a fungus at all, but a completely separate, extinct branch of complex life.
